title: Finding a theory of gravitation
part: Part II: Curvature and general relativity
one_line_summary: Opens Part II by extracting a programme for relativistic gravity from two principles, equivalence and general covariance: free fall erases gravity locally, tidal effects betray it, physics in curved spacetime follows from special-relativistic tensor laws by swapping eta for g, the metric becomes a field obeying a field equation, local flatness makes this precise, and gravitational time dilation and redshift are the first payoff.
role_in_book: Part I built special relativity, vectors, 1-forms, tensors and the metric in flat or merely curvilinear settings. This short, largely qualitative chapter is the hinge into Part II: it supplies the physical reasons why gravity should be geometry and sets the agenda (parallel transport and covariant derivatives in ch7, geodesics in ch8-9, measurements in orthonormal frames in ch10, Riemann in ch11, energy-momentum in ch12, the field equation in ch13). Its six numbered 'Lessons' are the contract the rest of the book fulfils, and its hand-waving estimates (light bending, clock rates) are explicitly redone properly in Part IV (ch21-24) and the local flatness claim is proved with Riemann normal coordinates in Part V (ch35).

learning_objectives: Reader can explain why Newton's instantaneous action at a distance is incompatible with the relativity of simultaneity.
Reader can state the weak and strong equivalence principles, say what separates them, and connect the weak form to m_i = m_g.
Reader can show by the Galilean coordinate change x' = x - g t^2/2 that a uniform gravitational field disappears from the equations of motion of an interacting particle cloud.
Reader can explain why only tidal (inhomogeneous) effects distinguish genuine gravity from an accelerating frame, and design a two-particle test for it.
Reader can define a local inertial frame and explain in what sense it is 'local' in space and time.

Reader can use the accelerating-rocket argument to predict that light bends in a gravitational field, estimate the solar deflection to order of magnitude, and say why this argument misses part of the full answer.
Reader can state the principle of general covariance and use index matching to spot a law that singles out a preferred basis or uses a non-scalar source.
Reader can explain why a Lorentz-invariant wave-equation upgrade of Poisson's equation with rho as source fails.
Reader can apply the eta -> g rule to promote a special-relativistic tensor law to one valid in the presence of gravity.
Reader can explain why the metric must satisfy a differential field equation and what role curvature plays in separating gravity from coordinate artefacts.
Reader can state the local flatness theorem (g = eta and first derivatives zero at a point, second derivatives not removable) and link second derivatives to curvature.
Reader can derive d tau = (1 - 2GM/r)^{1/2} dt from g_00 for a static clock, rewrite it in terms of escape speed or Schwarzschild radius, and expand it in the weak-field limit.
Reader can estimate gravitational redshift for Earth, Sun, white dwarf and neutron star surfaces and explain why GPS needs both SR and GR clock corrections.
Reader can distinguish Doppler, gravitational and cosmological redshift by their physical origin.

teaching_approach.summary: A conceptual chapter built around two guiding claims (you cannot feel your own weight in free fall; only the metric carries the influence of spacetime) and distilled into six numbered Lessons that act as a checklist for the whole of Part II. The authors alternate short boxed Examples with prose: an explicit Galilean coordinate change, a springs-in-a-box accelerometer, a spaceship tidal test, an accelerating rocket for light bending, a Machian interlude, a deliberately failed theory, and a clock-drop argument. The mathematics stays at the level of Part I (coordinate changes, index matching, one metric component), and rigorous versions are deferred with pointers to ch11, ch24 and ch35. Estimates are made with numerical factors thrown away openly, and the authors are candid when a heuristic under-counts (light bending). The chapter ends with a concrete, measurable consequence (gravitational time dilation, GPS) so that the abstract principles pay off.
narrative_arc: Part II roadmap: what chapters 6-14 will build towards (curvature on the left, energy-momentum on the right of Einstein's equation)
Motivating problem: Newtonian gravity acts instantaneously and so defines a universal 'now', which relativity forbids
Two guiding claims announced: equivalence (no felt weight in free fall) and general covariance (spacetime enters physics only through the metric)
Model: m_i = m_g makes gravitational acceleration a property of the coordinates; weak equivalence principle
Formal check: a Galilean change to a falling frame removes a uniform g from an interacting N-particle cloud (Example 6.1); accelerometer box (Example 6.2)
Generalization to the strong equivalence principle covering all non-gravitational laws; consequence that free fall follows timelike geodesics (Example 6.3)
Caveat and escape: a uniform field is indistinguishable from no field, but real fields are inhomogeneous, so tidal effects reveal gravity (Example 6.4, Fig. 6.2)
Lessons 1-3 codified: free fall along geodesics, local inertial frames, tidal detection over finite regions
Quick payoff: rocket thought experiment shows light must bend (Example 6.5); honest admission that the local argument misses the spatial-curvature part; crude solar estimate eqn (6.5)
Historical interlude: Mach's principle, inertial forces from distant matter, and why nonlinearity pushes us from particle interactions to local fields (Example 6.6)
General covariance stated; no preferred bases; a failed Lorentz-covariant scalar theory shows what goes wrong (Example 6.7)
Synthesis: a valid tensor law without gravity remains valid with gravity once eta is replaced by g (Lesson 4)

The metric as a field: invariant geometry requires g at different points to be related by a differential equation built from curvature (Riemann tensor); correspondence with Newton and SR (Fig. 6.4, Lesson 5)
Local flatness theorem: g = eta and dg = 0 achievable at a point, second derivatives not; local orthonormal frames as the place where measurements happen (Lesson 6)
Application: static clock rate from g_00, rederived by a dropped-clock argument; gravitational redshift, neutron stars, GPS; three kinds of redshift contrasted
signature_moves: Numbered 'Lessons' (1-6) that compress each conceptual step into a portable rule the later chapters cite
Turning a principle into an explicit coordinate transformation so the reader watches g vanish from an equation (Example 6.1)
Deliberately constructing a plausible but wrong theory (Poisson upgraded to a wave equation) and diagnosing its failure by transformation properties
Order-of-magnitude estimates that openly discard factors and then state the true factor (light bending off by 4)
Candid admission of where the equivalence-principle heuristic breaks: the photon samples enough space to feel spatial curvature
Reusing everyday settings as test beds for relativity: a car driving through vertical rain, an accelerometer made of springs, waking up in a spaceship
Deriving the same result twice by different routes (metric component g_00 and a falling-clock plus SR time dilation argument)
Anchoring the abstract to technology and precision measurement (LEP Earth tides, GPS, a 2022 strontium lattice clock exercise)
Commuting-limits diagram (Fig. 6.4) to place GR relative to Newtonian gravity, SR and Newtonian mechanics

sections.title: Part II opener: roadmap to the field equation
sections.summary: A one-page overview of Part II listing what each of chapters 6-14 contributes: equivalence principle, parallel transport and connection coefficients, geodesics, making local measurements, Riemann and Ricci curvature as the left side of Einstein's equation, the energy-momentum tensor as the right side, the field equation itself, and a tour of its successes.
