Signals that later Parts will unpack chapter 14's successes in detail

sections.title: Chapter opening: why Newtonian gravity must be replaced
sections.summary: After an Einstein epigraph linking equal inertial and gravitational mass to composition-independent free fall, the authors point out that Newton's instantaneous interaction singles out a universal time, contradicting relativity of simultaneity. Two guiding claims are set out: a falling person feels no weight (equivalence), and spacetime influences physics only through its metric (general covariance).
concepts: equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass
key_moves: Identify the conflict between instantaneous gravity and relative simultaneity
Announce equivalence and covariance as the two search principles and hint that they are linked

sections.title: Free fall and the equivalence principle
sections.summary: Setting m_i = m_g in Newton's equation makes the gravitational field equal to a coordinate acceleration, so a falling observer sees no gravity. The weak principle (mechanics only) is illustrated by transforming a uniformly accelerated interacting particle cloud into a falling frame and by a spring accelerometer that cannot tell acceleration from weight. The strong principle extends this to all laws in a small enough region, implying that free particles follow timelike geodesics. Because a uniform field can be transformed away completely, gravity is only detectable through inhomogeneity, i.e. tidal effects, as in the spaceship test. Lessons 1-3 summarize. The rocket argument then shows light must bend, gives the angle gx/c^2, and the authors admit this is only part of the full photon deflection before estimating the solar deflection as GM/(R c^2).
concepts: equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass
timelike geodesic as free-fall world line
key_moves: m_i = m_g turns g(x) into a coordinate acceleration
Galilean change x' = x - g t^2/2 removes g from an N-body equation of motion while leaving pair forces (which depend on differences) untouched
Promote from mechanics (weak) to all laws within a small region (strong)
Particle at rest in SR moves along the time axis, so by SEP free fall is along timelike geodesics
Uniform field = no field; inhomogeneity (tides) is the only local signature of real gravity
Lessons 1-3: geodesic free fall, LIFs obey SR, tidal detection over extended regions
Rocket crossing: straight path in inertial frame becomes parabola y = y0 - g x^2/(2v^2) in rocket frame; set v -> c to get bending angle gx/c^2
Crude solar estimate: g ~ GM/R^2 acting over length ~ R gives theta ~ GM/(R c^2), off from the true value by a factor 4

sections.title: Interlude: Mach's principle and the case for fields (Example 6.6)
sections.summary: A historical detour: inertial forces in non-inertial frames raise the question of what they are relative to. Mach's answer, acceleration relative to the average matter of the Universe, would make inertial forces real interactions between masses, with an electromagnetism-like static inverse-square part and a 1/r part for relative acceleration. Equivalence identifies the static part with gravity. The authors then argue that treating gravity as particle-particle interactions is hopeless because mass-energy, including interaction energy, is itself a source: the theory is nonlinear, so a local field description is needed.
key_moves: Pose the question of defining inertial frames without absolute space
Mach: judge acceleration relative to the 'fixed stars'
Model inertial force by analogy with electrostatics (1/r^2) and radiation (1/r)
Equivalence principle identifies the static inertial term with gravity
Nonlinearity (interaction energy gravitates) forces a switch from particle interactions to locally defined fields; contrast with linear electromagnetism

sections.title: Why general relativity?
sections.summary: General covariance is stated as the requirement that physical laws keep their form under arbitrary coordinate transformations, which rules out laws that single out particular components or bases. A tempting relativistic upgrade of Poisson's equation to a wave equation with mass density as source fails because density is not a scalar. Combining the equivalence principle (SR laws hold in a LIF) with covariance (form preserved in any coordinates) gives the key rule: a valid tensor equation without gravity remains valid with gravity, with geometry, via the replacement of eta by a position-dependent g, being the only change (Lesson 4).
concepts: minimal coupling via eta to g replacement
key_moves: State general covariance and interpret it as a ban on preferred bases
Illustrate with F = dp/dt (geometric) versus a component-picking pseudo-law
Build d'Alembertian version of Poisson's equation, eqn (6.6), and reject it because rho transforms as part of a tensor
Syllogism: SR law holds in LIF (equivalence) + form holds in all coordinates (covariance) => law holds with gravity
Lesson 4: gravity enters tensor laws only through eta -> g

sections.title: A differential equation to describe gravity
sections.summary: The metric computes intervals along curves, eqn (6.7). Because coordinate-independent geometric facts (circle ratios, triangle angle sums) must come out the same whichever coordinates are used, the values of g at neighbouring points cannot be arbitrary: g is a field obeying a differential field equation. That equation involves a curvature tensor (Riemann) built from g and its derivatives, and curvature, unlike coordinate artefacts, is the true signature of gravity. The theory must reduce to Newtonian gravity for weak fields and slow motion and to SR when gravity vanishes (Fig. 6.4). A margin note distinguishes a general LIF from the freely falling frame, which stays inertial along its geodesic for long proper times. Lesson 5: GR is a field theory of the metric.
concepts: line element and interval along a curve
frame of reference versus coordinate system
key_moves: Metric as a rulebook for intervals, eqn (6.7)
Coordinate-invariant geometric answers require g at different points to be related, hence a differential equation
Field viewpoint: input a spacetime point, output the tensor g there
Curvature (Riemann) as the part that no coordinate choice can remove
Constraint from correspondence: Newtonian limit and SR limit (Fig. 6.4)
Lesson 5: GR is a field theory of g(x)

sections.title: Local flatness
sections.summary: Minkowski spacetime is flat. By the equivalence principle every observer can treat spacetime as flat locally. The local flatness theorem says coordinates exist in which the metric equals eta at a chosen point (possible since a symmetric matrix can be diagonalized and normalized) and, more strongly, its first derivatives vanish there; second derivatives cannot generally be removed because they encode curvature. A LIF is a frame meeting both conditions at a point; the freely falling frame is the key example. Observers build orthonormal bases where they are, and all measurements are interpreted there with the Minkowski metric (Lesson 6).
key_moves: Equivalence principle => locally everyone can use flat spacetime
Condition 1: g_{mu nu}(P) = eta_{mu nu} by diagonalizing and rescaling
Condition 2: partial derivatives of g vanish at P, making flatness hold in an infinitesimal neighbourhood
Second derivatives are not removable and relate to curvature
Lesson 6: measurements are made in a local orthonormal frame using eta

sections.title: Time dilation in a gravitational field
sections.summary: For a static clock, only g_00 contributes, so proper tick interval is (-g_00)^{1/2} times coordinate interval. With the weak-field metric g_00 = -(1 - 2GM/r) this gives gravitational time dilation, rewritten via escape speed and Schwarzschild radius. A second derivation drops a clock from far away: it matches the distant clock at release, arrives at radius r with v^2 = 2GM/r, and the SR gamma factor between it and a static clock reproduces the same factor. Recast for atomic transitions this is gravitational redshift. The authors note the weak-field approximation 1 - GM/R, negligible effects on Earth, large effects on neutron stars, the GPS need for both SR and GR corrections, and contrast Doppler, gravitational and cosmological redshifts.
concepts: Doppler versus gravitational versus cosmological redshift
key_moves: Static clock: -d tau^2 = g_00 dt^2
Insert g_00 from eqn (5.22) with Phi = -GM/r
Identify 2GM/r = v_esc^2 and r_S = 2GM/c^2
Alternative route: free-falling clock is locally inertial; energy conservation gives its speed; SR gamma supplies the factor
Clocks -> atomic frequencies -> redshift
Binomial expansion for weak fields and survey of magnitudes (Earth, neutron star, GPS)
Classify redshifts by origin: velocity (Doppler) versus change of metric (gravitational, cosmological)

sections.title: Chapter summary and exercises
sections.summary: A three-point summary (equivalence principle in LIFs, general covariance, gravitational time dilation) and six exercises ranging from redshift estimates and a real optical-lattice clock measurement to satellite clock rates, Schwarzschild clock comparisons, radar-defined spatial distance in a general stationary metric, clock synchronization and the Sagnac effect.
concepts: spatial metric of a stationary spacetime
key_moves: Consolidate with numerical estimates
Extend the g_00 idea to metrics with g_0i cross terms via light-signal constructions

concepts.name: instantaneous action at a distance
concepts.definition: The Newtonian assumption that the gravitational force between bodies depends on their simultaneous positions, so a change in one source is felt everywhere at once; it presupposes an absolute simultaneity that special relativity denies.
concepts.how_introduced: The opening paragraph uses it as the reason a new theory is needed: instantaneous interaction picks out a universal time for all observers.

concepts.name: equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass
concepts.definition: The experimental fact that the mass resisting acceleration (inertial mass) equals the mass coupling to gravity (gravitational mass), so all bodies at a given place fall with the same acceleration regardless of composition.
concepts.how_introduced: Via the Einstein epigraph and eqn (6.1): cancelling m_i against m_g shows the field g(x) equals the particle's coordinate acceleration, suggesting gravity is a feature of the coordinates.

concepts.name: free fall
concepts.definition: Motion under the influence of gravity alone, with no non-gravitational forces acting; a freely falling observer carries no felt weight.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in a margin note and dramatized by the astronaut who, seeing no change in her rest-frame coordinates, concludes there is no gravity.

concepts.name: weak equivalence principle
concepts.definition: The statement that inertial and gravitational mass are identical, so that for purely mechanical motion one can choose coordinates in which a freely falling particle obeys the same laws as in unaccelerated Cartesian coordinates without gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced right after eqn (6.1); illustrated by transforming away a uniform field (Example 6.1) and by the spring accelerometer (Example 6.2). A margin note jokes that its weakness is that it covers only mechanics.
prerequisites: equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass

concepts.name: strong equivalence principle
concepts.definition: At any event in any gravitational field one can choose local coordinates such that, in a small enough neighbourhood, all laws of physics (not only mechanics) take their special-relativistic form without gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as a strengthening of the weak principle, boxed, and immediately used to deduce geodesic free fall (Example 6.3). The chapter summary phrases it as non-gravitational laws taking SR form in every LIF.
concepts.notes: Modern literature usually calls this (non-gravitational laws) the Einstein equivalence principle and reserves 'strong' for a version that includes gravitational self-energy and gravitational experiments; the book's usage differs.

concepts.name: uniformly accelerating reference frame
concepts.definition: A frame whose origin accelerates with constant acceleration relative to an inertial frame; in Newtonian kinematics reached by x' = x - (1/2) a t^2, t' = t, which adds a uniform fictitious acceleration -a to every body.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 6.1 applies it with a = g to an interacting N-particle cloud: the uniform gravitational term cancels while the pair forces, depending only on separations, are unchanged.

concepts.name: homogeneous gravitational field equivalence
aliases: uniform field is equivalent to no field
concepts.definition: A spatially uniform, constant gravitational field can be removed everywhere by passing to a single uniformly accelerating frame, so no experiment can distinguish it from acceleration; such a field carries no invariant gravitational content.
concepts.how_introduced: Emphasized after Example 6.3 as the apparently discouraging conclusion that seems to make gravity undetectable, before being rescued by the inhomogeneity of real fields.

concepts.name: tidal force
aliases: relative acceleration of nearby free particles
concepts.definition: The relative acceleration between nearby freely falling bodies caused by the variation of the gravitational field across the region they occupy; it cannot be transformed away by any choice of frame and is the local signature of genuine gravity (spacetime curvature).
concepts.how_introduced: Arises as the escape from the uniform-field paradox; Example 6.4 has an astronaut release two parallel test particles and watch whether their separation changes; a margin note connects to ocean tides and the Earth tide stretching the LEP ring.
concepts.notes: Formalized as geodesic deviation and the Riemann tensor in GA ch11 and ch35.

concepts.name: local inertial frame
concepts.definition: A frame, set up around an event, in which the metric takes the Minkowski form and its first derivatives vanish at that event, so that special-relativistic physics holds to first order in a sufficiently small neighbourhood; a freely falling, non-rotating laboratory realizes one.
concepts.how_introduced: Lesson 2 introduces it physically as the falling observer's laboratory; section 6.4 later gives the mathematical conditions (6.8) and (6.9).

concepts.name: local Lorentz frame
concepts.definition: A local inertial frame described with an orthonormal basis, so the metric components at the observer are exactly diag(-1,1,1,1); it is the frame in which an observer actually interprets measured components.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in a margin note on Lesson 2 and returned to as Lesson 6 with the picture of an observer's lab built from short rigid rods.

concepts.name: timelike geodesic as free-fall world line
concepts.definition: Freely falling particles move on timelike geodesics: world lines whose tangent is everywhere timelike and which are locally straight, i.e. straight time-axis world lines in each local inertial frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 6.3 argues that since a particle at rest in SR moves along the time axis, the strong equivalence principle implies free-fall paths are timelike curves (the book loosely calls such curves geodesics); Lesson 1 and a margin note contrast this with a Newtonian force from the Sun.
concepts.notes: The book's wording can suggest every timelike curve is a geodesic; only the unaccelerated ones are. Geodesics are developed in GA ch8-9.

concepts.name: gravitational deflection of light
concepts.definition: The change in direction of a light ray passing a massive body. The equivalence principle alone forces some bending; full GR predicts 4GM/(b c^2) for impact parameter b, twice the value obtained from the equivalence principle or Newtonian corpuscles, the extra half coming from spatial curvature.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 6.5 has a particle cross an accelerating rocket; in the rocket frame its path is a parabola, and replacing the particle by a photon and acceleration by gravity implies bending by angle about gx/c^2. A crude solar estimate follows, eqn (6.5).
concepts.notes: The book states the full photon effect is three times the heuristic value; the standard result is a factor of two (see gaps_and_pitfalls). Done properly in GA ch24 §24.1.

concepts.name: Mach's principle
concepts.definition: The idea that inertial frames, and hence inertial forces, are determined by acceleration relative to the averaged distribution of all matter in the Universe rather than relative to absolute space.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 6.6 poses how inertial frames can be defined without absolute space, gives Mach's answer, and sketches a speculative force law between inertial masses modelled on electromagnetism.
concepts.notes: Presented as an influence on Einstein; the chapter does not discuss how far GR actually realizes Mach's principle.

concepts.name: inertial forces
concepts.definition: Apparent forces proportional to mass, such as centrifugal force, that appear in Newton's laws written in accelerating or rotating frames.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivates the Mach interlude; a margin note gives centrifugal force as the example and points to ch8.

concepts.name: nonlinearity of gravitation
concepts.definition: Because all mass-energy sources gravity, including interaction energy and the energy of the gravitational field itself, gravitational fields do not superpose linearly; for example gravitational waves scatter off one another, unlike light waves in vacuum.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 6.6 uses it to explain why describing gravity as pairwise particle interactions becomes intractable; a margin note contrasts linear electromagnetism, whose waves are uncharged and pass through each other.

concepts.name: field description of gravity
concepts.definition: Describing an interaction through a field defined at each spacetime point, which each particle both sources and responds to locally, instead of direct influences between distant particles.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the escape from the nonlinear many-body bookkeeping of the Machian approach; later sharpened by the claim that the field in GR is the metric itself.

concepts.name: principle of general covariance
concepts.definition: Physical laws must be expressible in a form that is unchanged under arbitrary smooth coordinate transformations, which in practice means writing them as tensor equations with no preferred basis or components.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in the opening (spacetime acts only through the metric) and boxed in section 6.2 as the reason for the name 'general' relativity; illustrated by a law picking out the y-component and by the failed theory of Example 6.7.
concepts.notes: The book calls it a restatement of the equivalence principle; the physical content of general covariance by itself is debated (any theory can be written covariantly), a point not raised here.

concepts.name: manifestly covariant tensor equation
concepts.definition: An equation written entirely in terms of tensors with the same free indices on both sides, so that if it holds in one coordinate system it holds in all.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note to the Lesson 4 argument; motivated by contrasting F = dp/dt with a law that singles out one component.

concepts.name: failed scalar theory of gravity
concepts.definition: The guess that relativistic gravity is a scalar potential obeying the wave equation box Phi = 4 pi G rho. It fails because the source rho (mass density) is not a Lorentz scalar: it is one component of the energy-momentum tensor, so the equation cannot hold in every inertial frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 6.7 constructs it by replacing the Laplacian in Poisson's equation with the 4D d'Alembertian, then rejects it on transformation grounds; a margin note says the correct equation has curvature on the left and the energy-momentum tensor on the right.
concepts.notes: Our addition, not the book's: scalar theories of this type (e.g. Nordstrom's) also fail observationally, predicting no light bending. The book rejects the equation on transformation grounds alone.

concepts.name: minimal coupling via eta to g replacement
concepts.definition: The recipe for including gravity in non-gravitational physics: take a tensor law valid in special relativity and replace the Minkowski metric eta by the general metric g (and, as later chapters add, partial derivatives by covariant ones).
concepts.how_introduced: Derived as a syllogism: SR laws hold in a LIF by equivalence, and a tensor law keeps its form in every coordinate system by covariance, so the only trace of gravity is the altered geometry encoded in g.
concepts.notes: The need to replace derivatives with covariant derivatives is not mentioned here; it is the subject of GA ch7.

concepts.name: Minkowski metric
concepts.definition: The metric of flat spacetime with components diag(-1,1,1,1) in inertial Cartesian coordinates; described as the box of clocks and rulers of special relativity.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in section 6.2 as the metric used in a LIF, to be upgraded to g.

concepts.name: line element and interval along a curve
concepts.definition: The invariant length of a curve x^mu(lambda) computed by integrating the square root of the absolute value of g_{mu nu} (dx^mu/d lambda)(dx^nu/d lambda) along it.
concepts.how_introduced: Section 6.3 presents the metric as a rulebook for distances and angles and writes the integral (6.7).

concepts.name: metric as a field
concepts.definition: In GR the metric tensor is a dynamical field on spacetime, assigning a tensor g(x) to each event, and it is this field (not a force field) that carries gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Described as a machine that takes a spacetime point and returns the tensor there; a margin note warns against picturing gravity as a force field, and Lesson 5 codifies it.

concepts.name: field equation for the metric
concepts.definition: A differential equation that determines how the metric varies from point to point in terms of its sources, separating true gravitational effects from coordinate choices.
concepts.how_introduced: Argued for because coordinate-independent geometric statements (circumference/diameter = pi, triangle angle sums) require the values of g at different points to be related; its form is deferred to ch13.

concepts.name: Riemann curvature tensor
concepts.definition: A tensor built from the metric and its first and second derivatives whose non-vanishing signals intrinsic curvature of spacetime, which no coordinate change can remove.
concepts.how_introduced: Named as the tensor that the field equation is built from and identified with true gravitation; definition deferred to ch11.

concepts.name: correspondence limits of general relativity
concepts.definition: Any relativistic theory of gravity must reproduce Newtonian gravity for weak fields and slow motion and reduce to special relativity when gravity vanishes; Newtonian mechanics sits at the corner where both limits are taken.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as the one remaining clue for building the theory and displayed as a square of limits in Fig. 6.4.

concepts.name: frame of reference versus coordinate system
concepts.definition: A frame is a set of basis vectors defined at points, existing independently of any coordinate grid; coordinates are labels of events. Different frames can share coordinates and vice versa.
concepts.how_introduced: A margin note in section 6.4 draws the distinction and contrasts a general LIF (coordinate conditions at a point, achievable by Riemann normal coordinates) with the freely falling frame (basis e_t tangent to a geodesic).

concepts.name: freely falling frame
concepts.definition: A local frame whose time basis vector is the tangent to a free-fall geodesic; it remains locally inertial for the whole of that world line, so it is flat only in a small spatial region but for long stretches of proper time.
concepts.how_introduced: A margin note separates it from a general LIF defined at a single event; the main text calls it the key example of a LIF.
prerequisites: timelike geodesic as free-fall world line

concepts.name: flat spacetime
concepts.definition: Spacetime with no curvature, in which global coordinates exist making the metric equal to eta everywhere; used by observers not subject to gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening sentence of section 6.4.

concepts.name: local flatness theorem
concepts.definition: At any point P of a spacetime with Lorentzian metric one can choose coordinates such that g_{mu nu}(P) = eta_{mu nu} and all first partial derivatives of g_{mu nu} vanish at P; the second derivatives cannot in general all be set to zero, their residue being curvature.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the equivalence principle; the first condition justified by diagonalizing a symmetric matrix, the second asserted with a pointer to Riemann normal coordinates in ch35.
concepts.notes: No counting argument (40 first derivatives vs 40 free second-order coordinate coefficients; 100 second derivatives vs 80, leaving 20 curvature components) is given here.

concepts.name: Riemann normal coordinates
concepts.definition: A coordinate system built from geodesics radiating from a point, in which the metric is Minkowskian and its first derivatives vanish at that point.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in a margin note as the construction that realizes a general LIF; deferred to ch35.

concepts.name: Lorentz signature
concepts.definition: The pattern of one negative and three positive eigenvalues of the metric, which is preserved by any coordinate change and must be matched when normalizing a local frame to eta.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note to the local flatness theorem.

concepts.name: proper time
concepts.definition: The time recorded by an ideal clock along its world line, given by -d tau^2 = g_{alpha beta} dx^alpha dx^beta; for a clock at rest in coordinates it is (-g_00)^{1/2} dt.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 6.8 upgrades the SR relation between proper and coordinate time to the curved metric.

concepts.name: Newtonian limit of the metric
concepts.definition: For weak static fields the metric has g_00 = -(1 + 2 Phi) with Phi = -GM/r for a point mass (and g_ij = (1 - 2 Phi) delta_ij), valid when GM/(r c^2) << 1.
concepts.how_introduced: Imported from eqn (5.22) to evaluate g_00 near a star in Example 6.8; the authors caution the result assumes the Newtonian limit.

concepts.name: gravitational time dilation
aliases: clocks run slow in a potential well
concepts.definition: A clock held at rest deeper in a gravitational potential ticks more slowly, as compared by exchange of signals, than an identical clock far away; for a static clock outside a spherical mass d tau = (1 - 2GM/(r c^2))^{1/2} dt.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived twice in section 6.5: from g_00 of the weak-field metric, and by dropping a third clock from far away and applying SR time dilation at speed v = sqrt(2GM/r).
concepts.notes: Formula (6.11) is actually exact for static observers in Schwarzschild spacetime, eqn (6.14), even though here it is obtained in the weak-field limit.

concepts.name: escape velocity
concepts.definition: The minimum speed at distance r from a mass M that lets a projectile reach infinity, v_esc^2 = 2GM/r in Newtonian mechanics.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to reinterpret the time-dilation factor as the SR gamma for the escape speed, and in the clock-drop derivation as the speed of a clock falling from rest at infinity.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild radius
concepts.definition: The radius r_S = 2GM/c^2 associated with a mass M; the static time-dilation factor is sqrt(1 - r_S/r).
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as a convenient rewriting of eqn (6.11), with a pointer to Part IV.

concepts.name: gravitational redshift
concepts.definition: Light emitted by a source deeper in a gravitational potential is received by a higher observer at lower frequency (longer wavelength), by the same factor as gravitational time dilation.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by reinterpreting the clock argument in terms of atomic transition frequencies; applied to Earth, neutron stars and GPS, and to a millimetre-scale strontium clock experiment in Exercise 6.2.

concepts.name: Doppler versus gravitational versus cosmological redshift
concepts.definition: Doppler redshift comes from relative velocity of source and observer in flat spacetime; gravitational redshift from differences in the metric between emission and reception points in a static field; cosmological redshift from the expansion of space between emission and reception.
concepts.how_introduced: A closing paragraph of section 6.5 lists the three and groups the latter two as metric effects.

concepts.name: Global Positioning System relativistic corrections
concepts.definition: Satellite navigation requires correcting orbiting clocks for special-relativistic time dilation due to their motion (clocks run slow) and for gravitational blueshift due to their weaker gravitational potential (clocks run fast).
concepts.how_introduced: Cited in section 6.5 as the everyday technology where tiny gravitational redshift matters; Exercise 6.3 asks for the combined factor for a satellite.

concepts.name: spatial metric of a stationary spacetime
aliases: measured length in a metric with g_0i
concepts.definition: In a metric with time-space cross terms, the distance measured by bouncing light between neighbouring points is dl^2 = (g_ij - g_0i g_0j / g_00) dx^i dx^j.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 6.5 builds it from the round-trip light time between A and B (Fig. 6.6).
prerequisites: line element and interval along a curve

concepts.name: clock synchronization in stationary spacetimes
concepts.definition: Defining simultaneity with light signals in a metric with g_0i gives a time shift -g_0i dx^i/g_00 between neighbouring clocks; around a closed loop the shifts need not cancel, so global synchronization can fail (e.g. on a rotating disc).
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 6.6 develops it and applies it to the rotating frame metric.
prerequisites: spatial metric of a stationary spacetime

concepts.name: Sagnac effect
concepts.definition: Counter-propagating light beams around a rotating closed loop acquire a travel-time difference proportional to the rotation rate and enclosed area, giving an interference fringe shift of 4 pi Omega r^2/(lambda c) for a circular loop.
concepts.how_introduced: Final part of Exercise 6.6, derived from the synchronization discrepancy.

key_equations.name: Newtonian equation of motion with two masses
key_equations.meaning: Distinguishes the mass that resists acceleration from the mass that couples to gravity; equality makes the acceleration independent of the body.
key_equations.symbols: m_i inertial mass; m_g gravitational mass; g(x) gravitational field

key_equations.name: Equation of motion of one particle in an interacting cloud
key_equations.latex: m\frac{d^2\vec x}{dt^2} = m\vec g + \sum_{p=1}^{N-1}\vec F(\vec x-\vec x_p)
key_equations.meaning: One test particle feels the uniform gravitational field plus non-gravitational forces from the other N-1 particles that depend only on separations.
key_equations.symbols: x_p positions of the other particles; F pair force

key_equations.name: Transformation to the freely falling frame
key_equations.meaning: Galilean change to coordinates whose origin falls with acceleration g.
key_equations.symbols: primed quantities refer to the falling observer O'

key_equations.name: Equation of motion in the falling frame
key_equations.meaning: The uniform field has disappeared; the particle obeys the gravity-free law, demonstrating the (weak) equivalence principle.

key_equations.name: Parabolic path in the rocket frame
key_equations.latex: x = x_0 + vt,\quad y = y_0 - \tfrac12 g t^2\ \Rightarrow\ y = y_0 - \frac{g x^2}{2v^2}
key_equations.meaning: A particle moving straight in the inertial frame traces a downward parabola in a rocket accelerating upward at g.

key_equations.name: Local light-bending angle
key_equations.meaning: Setting v = c: after crossing a horizontal distance x in an effective field g, a light ray tilts by this angle.
key_equations.symbols: g acceleration or field; x horizontal distance

key_equations.name: Crude deflection of starlight by the Sun
key_equations.meaning: Order-of-magnitude deflection taking field GM/R^2 acting over a path length of order R; the true GR value is four times this.
key_equations.symbols: M_sun, R_sun solar mass and radius

key_equations.name: Machian inertial force ansatz
key_equations.meaning: Speculative electromagnetism-inspired form: a static inverse-square part identified with gravity plus a 1/r part for relative acceleration.

key_equations.name: Geometric form of Newton's second law
key_equations.meaning: Relation between vectors with no preferred basis; contrasted with a non-covariant law that singles out the y-component.

key_equations.name: d'Alembertian
key_equations.meaning: Lorentz-invariant generalization of the Laplacian used to build the failed theory.

key_equations.name: Failed relativistic Poisson equation
key_equations.meaning: Tempting wave-equation upgrade of Newtonian gravity; rejected because rho is not a scalar under Lorentz transformations.

key_equations.name: Lesson 4 replacement rule
key_equations.meaning: Gravity enters tensor laws by replacing the constant Minkowski metric with a position-dependent metric.

key_equations.name: Interval along a curve
key_equations.meaning: The metric turns a parametrized curve into an invariant length or proper time.

key_equations.name: Local flatness condition 1
key_equations.meaning: At any single point, coordinates can be chosen to make the metric Minkowskian.

key_equations.name: Local flatness condition 2
key_equations.meaning: First derivatives of the metric can also be made to vanish at that point; second derivatives cannot, and encode curvature.

key_equations.name: Proper time of a static clock
key_equations.meaning: For a clock at rest in the coordinates only the time-time metric component contributes.
key_equations.symbols: tau proper time; t coordinate time

key_equations.name: Gravitational time dilation
key_equations.meaning: A static clock at radius r ticks slower than coordinate (far-away) time; in SI units the factor is [1 - 2GM/(c^2 r)]^{1/2}.
key_equations.symbols: c = 1; M mass of the star; r radial distance; g_00 time-time metric component

key_equations.name: Escape-velocity form
key_equations.meaning: The time-dilation factor equals the SR gamma factor evaluated at the escape speed.

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild-radius form
key_equations.meaning: Same factor expressed with the Schwarzschild radius.

key_equations.name: SR time dilation in the clock-drop argument
key_equations.meaning: Kinetic energy gained in falling from rest at infinity fixes the speed; the SR gamma between falling and static clocks supplies the factor.

key_equations.name: Time dilation rederived
key_equations.meaning: Result of the falling-clock argument, identical to (6.11).

key_equations.name: Weak-field expansion
key_equations.meaning: Binomial approximation of the time-dilation factor when GM/(Rc^2) << 1 (the book writes 1 - GM/R in c = 1 units).

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild line element
key_equations.meaning: Metric outside a spherically symmetric star, given in Exercise 6.4 for comparing clocks at two radii.

key_equations.name: Satellite versus polar clock rate (Exercise 6.3)
key_equations.meaning: Combines the gravitational blueshift of the higher clock with the SR slowing due to orbital motion (v^2 = GM/r for a circular orbit); the two rates agree when r = 3R/2.
key_equations.symbols: R planet radius; r orbit radius

key_equations.name: Coordinate time for a light signal in a general metric
key_equations.meaning: Solving ds^2 = 0 for dt gives the two coordinate-time intervals for a null displacement dx^i (future- and past-directed).

key_equations.name: Round-trip time for a radar signal
key_equations.meaning: Round-trip interval for light from A to B and back. As printed this is the coordinate-time round trip; the proper time at A needs an extra factor (-g_00)^{1/2}, i.e. 2[...]^{1/2}/(-g_00)^{1/2}, which is what yields (6.17).

key_equations.name: Spatial metric from radar ranging
key_equations.meaning: Physical distance between neighbouring points in a stationary spacetime, as measured by light round trips.

key_equations.name: Synchronized time on A's world line
key_equations.meaning: Time on A simultaneous with event x^0 on B, defined as midway between emission and reception.

key_equations.name: Synchronization discrepancy around a rotating loop
key_equations.meaning: Going once around a circle in a rotating frame, the synchronization offsets accumulate to a non-zero total (the printed integral omits d phi).
key_equations.symbols: Omega angular velocity; r radius; c = 1

key_equations.name: Sagnac fringe shift
key_equations.meaning: Interference shift between counter-propagating beams in a rotating circular fibre (divide by c in SI units).

figures.label: Fig. 6.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: An accelerometer: a mass held at the centre of a box by light springs.
figures.visual_description: Line drawing of a transparent cube (hidden edges dotted) with a small ball at its centre attached to the middle of each face by six coiled springs, two vertical, two horizontal left-right and two receding in depth.
figures.what_it_teaches: The displacement of a spring-suspended mass reads out acceleration, but the same displacement is produced by gravity, so the device cannot tell the two apart (weak equivalence).

redesign.idea: Equivalence accelerometer: a 3D spring-mass box that the learner can place on a planet, in a thrusting rocket, or in free fall, with a readout of spring displacement that is identical in the planet and rocket cases and zero in free fall.
redesign.interaction: Toggle scenario (planet surface with g slider / rocket with thrust slider / orbiting or falling); drag the box sideways to add horizontal acceleration; displacement vector and 'measured g' update live; a hidden-label quiz asks the learner to guess which scenario produced a reading.

figures.label: Fig. 6.2(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Panel (a): in a uniform field, two side-by-side test particles accelerate in the same direction on parallel paths.
figures.visual_description: Label '(a)' and two small open circles placed side by side, each with a straight vertical arrow pointing straight down; the arrows are parallel.
figures.what_it_teaches: Uniform fields produce identical accelerations that a single frame change removes.

redesign.idea: Combined into the tidal-test demo described for Fig. 6.2(b).

figures.label: Fig. 6.2(a) floor
figures.caption_paraphrase: Grey slab beneath panel (a) representing a flat surface or ship floor producing a uniform field.
figures.visual_description: A plain light-grey horizontal rectangle with no labels; in the printed layout it sits under the two parallel arrows of panel (a).
figures.what_it_teaches: Stands for the source of a uniform field (effectively an infinite flat slab or an accelerating floor).

redesign.idea: Decorative element; absorbed into the Fig. 6.2(b) demo as the 'uniform field' source option.

figures.label: Fig. 6.2(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Panel (b): above a planet, two side-by-side test particles released on parallel paths drift towards each other, revealing a tidal force.
figures.visual_description: Label '(b)' and two small open circles side by side, each with an arrow pointing down but tilted inward so that the two arrows converge towards a point below.
figures.what_it_teaches: Real fields point towards a centre, so horizontally separated falling particles converge: an effect no uniform acceleration can mimic.

redesign.idea: Tidal test lab: a spaceship cabin with two (or a ring of) test particles released at rest; the learner chooses whether the ship is accelerating in empty space or hovering above a planet and watches separations evolve, with the planet able to be shrunk to a slab of infinite radius.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for planet radius/mass, cabin size, release separation and orientation (horizontal vs vertical pair); play/pause time; plot of separation versus time showing constant (uniform), converging (horizontal pair) or diverging (vertical pair); a 'cabin shrink' slider shows the effect vanishing as size -> 0.

figures.label: Fig. 6.2(b) planet
figures.caption_paraphrase: Grey arc beneath panel (b) representing the curved surface of a planet.
figures.visual_description: A light-grey filled segment of a large circle (a dome-shaped cap) with no labels, placed below the converging arrows in panel (b).
figures.what_it_teaches: Indicates a finite spherical source whose field lines are radial rather than parallel.

redesign.idea: Decorative element; represented by the adjustable planet in the Fig. 6.2(b) demo.

figures.label: Fig. 6.3(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Snapshots in an inertial frame of a rocket accelerating upward while a particle crosses it horizontally through side windows.
figures.visual_description: Four copies of a simple rocket (rectangular body, grey triangular nose, two nozzles) drawn left to right, each higher than the one before, with the vertical gaps growing. To the left of each rocket a star marks the particle source, and a horizontal arrow at the same fixed height shows the particle's straight path. From one snapshot to the next the arrow reaches further across the rocket body while the rocket rises past it.
figures.what_it_teaches: In the inertial frame the particle goes straight; the rocket's upward acceleration makes the crossing point drift lower relative to the rocket body.

redesign.idea: Two-frame rocket crossing: split screen showing the same event sequence in the inertial frame (rocket rising, straight particle path) and in the rocket frame (parabolic path), with a switch that replaces the rocket's thrust by a planet's gravity to show the cabin view is unchanged.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for rocket acceleration g, particle speed v (up to c) and cabin width; scrubbable time; overlay of y = y0 - g x^2/(2v^2) and the exit angle g x / v^2; toggle 'thrust' vs 'parked on planet'; numerical readout of the drop, which is invisible at v = c for everyday g to motivate the cosmic estimate.

figures.label: Fig. 6.3(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: In the rocket's own frame the crossing particle follows a parabola bending downward.
figures.visual_description: A single upright rocket with label '(b)'; inside, a curve starts horizontally at the left wall near the top and bends downward, meeting the right wall well below its entry height.
figures.what_it_teaches: The accelerated observer sees a curved trajectory; by equivalence, so would an observer at rest in a gravitational field, even for light.

redesign.idea: Merged with the Fig. 6.3(a) split-screen demo (rocket-frame pane).

figures.label: Fig. 6.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: A square of limits connecting general relativity, special relativity, Newtonian gravity and Newtonian mechanics.
figures.visual_description: Commutative-diagram layout: top-left 'General Relativity', top-right 'Newtonian Gravity', bottom-left 'Special Relativity', bottom-right 'Newtonian Mechanics'. Horizontal arrows point right labelled v -> 0; vertical arrows point down labelled G -> 0.
figures.what_it_teaches: GR must reduce to Newtonian gravity for slow motion and to SR when gravity is switched off, with Newtonian mechanics reached by both routes.

redesign.idea: Theory map: a clickable plane with axes 'speed v/c' and 'field strength GM/(rc^2)', shaded regions for the four theories, and example systems (GPS satellite, Mercury, binary pulsar, neutron star surface, black-hole merger) plotted as dots; clicking a dot shows which terms matter.
redesign.interaction: Hover to see each theory's governing equation; drag a probe point to read the size of v^2/c^2 and GM/(rc^2) corrections; arrows animate the limiting process along each edge (including c -> infinity as the cleaner label for v -> 0).

figures.label: Fig. 6.5(a) clocks 1 and 3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Part of panel (a): identical clocks 1 and 3 side by side far from the star just before clock 3 is released.
figures.visual_description: Two hand-drawn trapezoid-shaped alarm clocks labelled 1 and 3, both showing similar times, sitting next to each other with no motion lines.
figures.what_it_teaches: At release the falling clock is at rest beside the distant clock and ticks in step with it.

redesign.idea: Part of the clock-drop demo described under Fig. 6.5 (panel b).

figures.label: Fig. 6.5(a) clock 2 and star
figures.caption_paraphrase: Lower part of panel (a): clock 2 held fixed at distance r above the star.
figures.visual_description: A hand-drawn clock labelled 2 on a dashed horizontal line, a vertical double-headed arrow labelled r spanning down to a second dashed line through a small spiky sun labelled STAR.
figures.what_it_teaches: Sets up the static clock whose rate is to be compared, at radius r from the mass.

redesign.idea: Part of the clock-drop demo described under Fig. 6.5 (panel b).

figures.label: Fig. 6.5(b) clock 1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Upper part of panel (b): clock 1 remains far from the star after clock 3 has fallen. (The inventory attaches the Fig. 6.5 caption to this fragment.)
figures.visual_description: A single small hand-drawn clock labelled 1, alone.
figures.what_it_teaches: The reference clock far away keeps coordinate time.

redesign.idea: Part of the clock-drop demo described under Fig. 6.5 (panel b).

figures.label: Fig. 6.5(b) clocks 2 and 3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Lower part of panel (b): clock 3 arrives beside clock 2 moving at speed v towards the star.
figures.visual_description: Hand-drawn clock 2 on a dashed line and, to its right, clock 3 drawn with vertical speed lines above it and a downward arrow labelled v; a double-headed arrow r runs down to the dashed line through the spiky STAR.
figures.what_it_teaches: The falling clock passes the static clock at speed v with v^2 = 2GM/r; SR time dilation between them reproduces the gravitational factor.

redesign.idea: Clock-drop comparator: three clocks on a radial line above a star; clock 3 is released from far away and falls while tick marks from each clock are emitted as dots on a shared timeline, with a panel comparing the gravitational factor from g_00 and the SR gamma from the fall speed.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for stellar compactness GM/(rc^2) (Earth to neutron star) and radius of clock 2; play the drop; readouts of v/c, gamma^-1, (1-2GM/rc^2)^{1/2}; a toggle that starts the drop from finite height to show the two numbers no longer agree, exposing the heuristic's assumption.

figures.label: Fig. 6.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: A light signal sent from observer A to observer B and reflected back (for Exercises 6.5 and 6.6).
figures.visual_description: Spacetime diagram with two vertical world lines labelled A (left) and B (right). A dotted arrow runs up and right from A at time x^0 + dx^0_1 to B at time x^0, and a second dotted arrow runs up and left from B back to A, arriving at x^0 + dx^0_2.
figures.what_it_teaches: Radar ranging defines distance (half the round-trip time) and simultaneity (the midpoint on A's world line) in a general stationary metric.
concepts: spatial metric of a stationary spacetime

redesign.idea: Radar in a tilted spacetime: a 2D spacetime diagram where the learner sets metric components g_00, g_01, g_11 and watches the light cones tilt, the outgoing and returning null legs become unequal, and the midpoint-simultaneity mark shift; a rotating-disc mode chains segments around a loop to show the Sagnac mismatch.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for metric components (or rotation rate Omega and radius r); drag B's separation; readouts of coordinate round-trip, proper round-trip, measured dl and synchronization offset; loop mode accumulates offset and fringe count Delta N.

worked_examples.label: Example 6.1
worked_examples.problem: Show that a uniform gravitational field can be removed from the equations of motion of a particle in a cloud of N interacting test particles by moving to a freely falling frame.
worked_examples.method: Write Newton's law with a uniform gravity term plus pairwise forces depending on separations; apply the Galilean accelerating transformation x' = x - g t^2/2; the second time derivative subtracts g while separations are unchanged.
worked_examples.key_insight: Because gravity gives every particle the same acceleration (m_i = m_g), it can be absorbed into the frame; interactions that depend only on relative positions are blind to the change.
worked_examples.result: Equation (6.4): the particle obeys the gravity-free equation with only interparticle forces.

worked_examples.label: Example 6.2
worked_examples.problem: Use a mass suspended by springs inside a box (Fig. 6.1) to illustrate the equivalence principle.
worked_examples.method: Describe how acceleration in +x shifts the mass towards -x, and note that a gravitational field produces an identical displacement.
worked_examples.key_insight: An accelerometer measures the combination of acceleration and gravity, not either separately; in free fall it reads zero.

worked_examples.label: Example 6.3
worked_examples.problem: Deduce from special relativity what path freely falling particles follow in the presence of gravity.
worked_examples.method: In SR a particle at rest moves along its time axis, a timelike straight line; by the strong equivalence principle the same holds in the falling LIF, so globally free fall traces timelike curves that are locally straight.
worked_examples.key_insight: The equivalence principle lets a gravity-free SR fact become a statement about gravity: free fall is geodesic motion.
concepts: timelike geodesic as free-fall world line

worked_examples.label: Example 6.4
worked_examples.problem: An astronaut feels pressed into bed on waking: is the ship accelerating or near a planet?
worked_examples.method: Release two test particles moving initially parallel; watch whether their separation changes.
worked_examples.key_insight: A planet's field is inhomogeneous, so tidal convergence or divergence reveals gravity, while a pure acceleration leaves the separation fixed.
worked_examples.result: Any change in separation signals a tidal force and hence real gravity.

worked_examples.label: Example 6.5
worked_examples.problem: Show using an accelerating rocket that a gravitational field bends light.
worked_examples.method: In the inertial frame a particle crosses the rocket in a straight line; transform to the rocket frame to get the parabola y = y0 - g x^2/(2v^2); invoke equivalence to replace acceleration by a gravitational field; set v = c to get a tilt angle |dy/dx| = g x/c^2.
worked_examples.key_insight: Anything that moves straight in an inertial frame curves in an accelerated one, and equivalence transfers this to gravity, so even light must bend; the local argument, however, captures only the time-part of curvature.
worked_examples.result: Bending angle about g x/c^2; authors state the full effect near a spherical mass is larger because spatial curvature also contributes.

worked_examples.problem: Crude estimate of how much the Sun deflects starlight that grazes its limb. In the printed layout this is still inside the Example 6.5 box, which closes after the factor-of-4 remark.
worked_examples.method: Take the field at the surface g = GM/R^2, assume it acts over a path of order R, insert into theta ~ g x/c^2 and discard numerical factors.
worked_examples.key_insight: Dimensional reasoning with the equivalence-principle result already captures the scaling GM/(R c^2); only the numerical factor needs full GR.
worked_examples.result: theta ~ GM_sun/(R_sun c^2), eqn (6.5), about 2.1e-6 rad or 0.44 arcsec (our evaluation); the true value is four times larger, about 1.75 arcsec.

worked_examples.label: Example 6.6
worked_examples.problem: How can inertial frames be defined without absolute space, and what would a Machian theory of inertial forces look like?
worked_examples.method: Adopt Mach's criterion of non-acceleration relative to distant matter; model inertial interactions by analogy with electromagnetism (static inverse-square term, 1/r term for relative acceleration); identify the static part with gravity via equivalence; then observe that mass-energy including interaction energy gravitates, making a pairwise description nonlinear and unmanageable.
worked_examples.key_insight: Nonlinearity is what pushes gravitational theory from action between particles to local fields.

worked_examples.label: Example 6.7
worked_examples.problem: Test whether upgrading Poisson's equation to a Lorentz-invariant wave equation gives an acceptable theory of gravity.
worked_examples.method: Replace the Laplacian with the d'Alembertian to get eqn (6.6), then check transformation properties of each side.
worked_examples.key_insight: The left side transforms as a scalar but the mass density rho is a component of the energy-momentum tensor, so the equation holds only in one frame; a correct theory needs a tensor source and a tensorial left side involving curvature.
worked_examples.result: The equation is rejected, though it points towards a tensor equation with energy-momentum as source.

worked_examples.label: Example 6.8
worked_examples.problem: Find how the ticks of a clock at rest at distance r from a star compare with coordinate time.
worked_examples.method: Write -d tau^2 = g_00 dt^2 for a static clock; use g_00 = -(1 - 2GM/r) from the weak-field metric; take the square root; interpret the factor using escape velocity and the Schwarzschild radius.
worked_examples.key_insight: Gravitational time dilation follows from nothing more than one metric component: the metric is what connects coordinate labels to what clocks read.

worked_examples.problem: Rederive gravitational time dilation without the metric, using three identical clocks and a star (Fig. 6.5).
worked_examples.method: Clock 3 is released at rest next to distant clock 1 so they agree; it falls freely and is locally inertial so its tick interval is unchanged; Newtonian energy conservation gives v^2 = 2GM/r when it passes static clock 2; SR time dilation with gamma(v) relates the two, giving (6.13).
worked_examples.key_insight: Equivalence lets a freely falling clock act as an unbiased intermediary, converting a gravitational comparison into an SR velocity comparison.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: A mass held by springs is displaced equally by acceleration and by gravity, so a box observer cannot separate them.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: It illustrates only mechanics; in free fall it reads zero even near a planet, and a large box with two masses would detect tides, which the analogy does not show.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Pair the box demo with a two-box version separated vertically that shows differing readings in a planetary field.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A car accelerating through vertical rain
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Rain falling straight down appears to slant and curve on the windows of an accelerating car, the same kinematics as the rocket crossing rotated by 90 degrees.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Nothing relativistic or gravitational is involved; it conveys only the frame-dependence of trajectories, not why light obeys it.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Short animation morphing the rain-on-car view into the rocket-and-photon view by a 90-degree rotation.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Metric as a box of clocks and rulers / a rulebook
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The metric is what tells an observer how to convert coordinate displacements into measured times, lengths and angles.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Suggests a rigid measuring apparatus; in curved spacetime there is no global set of rulers, only local ones, and coordinates themselves carry no metric meaning.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A field as a machine: put in a point, get out a tensor
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Clarifies that g(x) is an assignment of a tensor to each spacetime point, with a field equation constraining how the outputs vary.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Does not convey that the field is dynamical and self-interacting.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Hover-probe over a 2D spacetime patch returning the local metric matrix and drawing the corresponding light cone.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Electromagnetism: Coulomb's law and radiation from accelerated charges
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Suggests a static inverse-square inertial interaction plus a 1/r term for relative acceleration, as with charges.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Gravity is not a vector-like force theory, and GR does not straightforwardly implement Mach's principle; the analogy is speculative.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Light waves pass through each other because they carry no charge, while gravitational waves carry energy and therefore source further gravity.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Photon-photon scattering exists quantum mechanically; the contrast is classical.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Side-by-side wave-packet collision: EM packets superpose and pass; gravitational packets pick up a small scattered component as amplitude increases.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Newton's Sun pulling the Earth versus the Earth falling freely along a geodesic
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: timelike geodesic as free-fall world line
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Reframes orbital motion as force-free free fall along a spacetime path that happens to circle the Sun.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The spatial orbit is not itself a geodesic of space; the geodesic is the helical world line in spacetime.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: 3D spacetime helix of Earth's world line around the Sun's world line, with a toggle showing the Newtonian force arrow disappear in the geodesic view.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A laboratory built from short rigid rods
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Pictures measurement as done with a small orthonormal frame at the observer's location.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Rigid rods are an idealization and must be short relative to the curvature scale.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Escape speed as a stand-in for gravitational time dilation
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The gravitational factor equals the SR factor at the speed needed to escape to infinity, linking gravity to familiar kinematic dilation.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The coincidence is special to Schwarzschild static observers; it is not a general rule for arbitrary metrics.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A law that singles out the y-component 'smells a rat'
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: An equation privileging one axis would look different after a rotation, showing why laws must be built from geometric objects.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Rotational covariance is a much weaker requirement than covariance under arbitrary coordinate changes.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Gravity and acceleration are exactly the same thing everywhere, so gravity is 'just' a choice of frame.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The equivalence holds only in a small enough region; real fields vary in space and their tidal effects cannot be removed by any frame, which is what curvature captures.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter first stresses sameness (Einstein's insight that gravity and an accelerating coordinate system are the same thing, the falling astronaut, the spring accelerometer) and only afterwards brings in the tidal caveat.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A uniform gravitational field is a physically real gravitational field detectable by local experiments.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A strictly uniform field can be transformed away everywhere at once; it has no invariant content.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Textbook problems routinely treat g as uniform near Earth's surface.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The rocket/equivalence argument gives the full deflection of starlight by the Sun.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It gives only the contribution from the time-time part of the metric; spatial curvature adds an equal amount, so the observed deflection is twice the equivalence-principle value (the book says three times, which is incorrect).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The argument is clean and yields the correct scaling GM/(bc^2).

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Light bending in the accelerating rocket is a special-relativistic effect.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The rocket is barely moving; the bending is pure kinematics of an accelerated frame, as with rain seen from an accelerating car.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Light and relativity are strongly associated in learners' minds.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: 'General relativity' is a generalization of the relativity principle to a broader class of relative motions.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The name reflects general covariance; the theory is a theory of gravity, not a more general relativity of motion.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The names 'special' and 'general' suggest a hierarchy of relativity principles.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Making Poisson's equation Lorentz-invariant with a d'Alembertian is enough for relativistic gravity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Mass density is a component of the energy-momentum tensor, so the source is not a scalar; a tensor equation with curvature is needed.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The same trick works for electromagnetic potentials in Lorenz gauge.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Gravity is a force field permeating spacetime, like an electric field.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In GR the gravitational field is the metric itself; free fall involves no force.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Newtonian intuition and the name 'gravitational field'.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: With a clever enough coordinate choice you can make spacetime flat around a point to all orders.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only the metric and its first derivatives can be matched to Minkowski at a point; second derivatives carry curvature that no coordinate change removes.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The equivalence principle seems to say gravity can always be transformed away.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A frame of reference and a coordinate system are the same thing.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A frame is a choice of basis vectors at points; coordinates label events; they are independent choices.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In SR inertial frames come with their own Cartesian coordinates, blurring the distinction.
concepts: frame of reference versus coordinate system

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Gravitational redshift is a kind of Doppler shift.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Doppler redshift comes from relative velocity; gravitational (and cosmological) redshift arises from the metric differing between emission and reception, with source and receiver at rest.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Both show up as frequency shifts of spectral lines and can mimic each other in data.
concepts: Doppler versus gravitational versus cosmological redshift

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Astronauts in orbit are weightless because gravity is negligible at their altitude.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Gravity there is only about 10 percent weaker than at the surface; they feel weightless because they are in free fall.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Everyday language of 'zero gravity' and the word 'weightless'.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Every timelike curve is a geodesic.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Timelike curves include accelerated world lines; only those with zero 4-acceleration (locally straight) are geodesics.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Example 6.3 phrases the conclusion in a way that seems to equate the two.
concepts: timelike geodesic as free-fall world line

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A clock near a massive body 'feels' its time slow down locally.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Locally every clock ticks at its normal proper rate; time dilation is a comparison between separated observers via signals.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Popular accounts describe time 'flowing slower' near a mass as if it were a local sensation.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: GPS satellite clocks run slow because of their orbital speed, so the GR correction is minor.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The gravitational blueshift (clocks fast by about 45 microseconds per day) outweighs the velocity effect (slow by about 7), for a net gain of about 38 microseconds per day (our figures, not the book's).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Special-relativistic time dilation is the better-known effect.

thought_experiments.name: Falling astronaut who cannot feel her weight
thought_experiments.setup: An astronaut in free fall watches her own coordinates in her rest frame and notices no change.
thought_experiments.lesson: Free fall removes the local sensation and local evidence of gravity.
thought_experiments.app_idea: First-person falling-lab view where released objects float; a toggle reveals the external view with the lab and objects falling together.

thought_experiments.name: Waking up in a spaceship
thought_experiments.setup: An astronaut pressed into bed releases two parallel test particles to decide between acceleration and a nearby planet.
thought_experiments.lesson: Tidal behaviour of initially parallel particles distinguishes real gravity from acceleration.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Game: learner is given an unlabeled cabin and must design a measurement (particle placement, waiting time) to decide the situation within a limited budget.

thought_experiments.name: Particle crossing an accelerating rocket
thought_experiments.setup: A particle or photon enters one window of a rocket accelerating at g and exits lower on the opposite wall.
thought_experiments.lesson: Straight paths curve in accelerated frames; by equivalence, gravity bends light.

thought_experiments.name: When the subway jerks (Mach)
thought_experiments.setup: Passengers thrown by a jerking train are imagined as being acted on by the distant stars relative to which the train accelerates.
thought_experiments.lesson: Mach's view makes inertial forces an interaction with distant matter, motivating Einstein.

thought_experiments.name: Dropping a clock from far away
thought_experiments.setup: Three identical clocks: one far from a star, one held at radius r, and one released from beside the first to fall past the second.
thought_experiments.lesson: A freely falling clock links a gravitational rate comparison to an SR velocity comparison, reproducing the time-dilation factor.

thought_experiments.name: Radar ranging and clock synchronization in a general metric
thought_experiments.setup: Observer A bounces a light signal off B and uses the round-trip time for distance and the midpoint for simultaneity; repeated around a rotating loop.
thought_experiments.lesson: Distance and simultaneity are observer constructions; with g_0i terms synchronization around a closed loop fails, giving the Sagnac effect.
concepts: spatial metric of a stationary spacetime

historical_notes.event: Chapter epigraph in which Einstein ties the equality of inertial and gravitational mass to the composition-independence of gravitational acceleration.
historical_notes.significance: Frames the equivalence principle as grounded in an experimental coincidence Newton left unexplained.

historical_notes.event: Mach proposed that inertial frames are defined relative to the average matter of the Universe, an idea that influenced Einstein's thinking toward the equivalence principle.
historical_notes.significance: Shows the philosophical route to GR and motivates treating inertial effects as physical interactions; Mach's dates (1838-1916) are given in a margin note.

historical_notes.event: A margin note gives a quip, attributed to Mach by Philipp Frank, that a jerking subway throws you down because of the fixed stars.

Deflection of starlight near the Sun during a total solar eclipse was measured early in the history of relativity and was an initial vindication of Einstein's ideas (the 1919 expeditions, a date not given in the text).
historical_notes.significance: Connects the rocket argument to the observation that made GR famous.

historical_notes.event: The interference shift of counter-rotating light beams on a rotating loop is named after Sagnac (1869-1928), in Exercise 6.6.
historical_notes.significance: Links clock-synchronization failure in rotating frames to a laboratory effect used in optical gyroscopes.

historical_notes.event: Exercise 6.2 cites a strontium optical-lattice clock experiment (Nature 602, 420) resolving gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale atomic sample.
historical_notes.significance: Shows gravitational redshift is now measurable over laboratory distances.

applications_and_observations.topic: Ocean tides and the Earth tide at CERN's LEP collider
applications_and_observations.details: Tidal forces from Sun and Moon raise ocean tides and also slightly deform the solid Earth; the Earth tide changed the circumference of the Large Electron-Positron collider by millimetres, which had to be corrected for.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: LEP circumference about 27 km; stretching of a few mm (book's figures)

applications_and_observations.topic: Deflection of starlight by the Sun
applications_and_observations.details: Crude equivalence-principle estimate theta ~ GM/(R c^2) from eqn (6.5), stated to be low by a factor of 4 relative to GR.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our evaluation: GM_sun/(R_sun c^2) = 2.1e-6 rad = 0.44 arcsec; GR value 4 times this = 1.75 arcsec

applications_and_observations.topic: Gravitational redshift at Earth's surface and on a neutron star
applications_and_observations.details: Negligible for an Earth-surface clock relative to deep space, but very large at the surface of a neutron star of about 1.4 solar masses and 10 km radius.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our evaluation: Earth GM/(Rc^2) ~ 7e-10; neutron star 2GM/(Rc^2) ~ 0.41, rate factor ~ 0.77, redshift z ~ 0.31

applications_and_observations.details: Positioning depends on precise timing; satellite clocks need an SR correction for orbital motion and a GR correction because they sit higher in Earth's potential.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Standard values (not in the book): gravitational +45 microseconds/day, velocity -7 microseconds/day, net about +38 microseconds/day

applications_and_observations.topic: Surface redshift of Earth, Sun and a white dwarf (Exercise 6.1)
applications_and_observations.details: Students estimate the fractional clock slowdown on three bodies.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our evaluation of GM/(Rc^2): Earth 7.0e-10; Sun 2.1e-6; 1 solar-mass white dwarf with R = 1000 km 1.5e-3

applications_and_observations.topic: Millimetre-scale redshift in a strontium lattice clock (Exercise 6.2)
applications_and_observations.details: Ultracold 87Sr atoms (about 100 nK) in an optical lattice resolve a frequency gradient across the sample; students compare with g/c^2.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Measured gradient about -1.0(2)e-19 per mm; our evaluation g/c^2 = 1.09e-19 per mm, consistent

applications_and_observations.details: Combining gravitational and orbital-speed effects gives a net rate difference that vanishes for an orbit of radius 3R/2 and is positive for higher orbits.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our evaluation for geostationary orbit (r = 42,164 km, R = 6,371 km): satellite clock fast by about 5.4e-10 (roughly 46 microseconds/day)

applications_and_observations.topic: Sagnac effect in a rotating fibre loop (Exercise 6.6)
applications_and_observations.details: Counter-propagating beams in a rotating circular fibre shift in phase by an amount proportional to rotation rate and enclosed area, the principle of fibre-optic and ring-laser gyroscopes.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Delta N = 4 pi Omega r^2/(lambda c) in SI units

notation_and_conventions.convention: Minkowski metric eta = diag(-1, 1, 1, 1) (mostly plus), with index 0 the time coordinate.
notation_and_conventions.notes: A margin note stresses that local frames must reproduce this Lorentz pattern of signs.

notation_and_conventions.convention: c = 1 throughout the time-dilation discussion; the factor becomes [1 - 2GM/(c^2 r)]^{1/2} with c restored. Exercise 6.4 uses G = c = 1.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Eqn (6.6) and the weak-field expansion mix conventions (1/c^2 appears in (6.6) though the d'Alembertian was defined with c = 1).

notation_and_conventions.convention: -d tau^2 = g_{alpha beta} dx^alpha dx^beta, so d tau^2 = -ds^2 for timelike intervals.
Written as T(x), with x either an abstract point P or its coordinates x^mu(P) = (t(P), x(P), y(P), z(P)); tensors in bold (eta, g, R).
m_i inertial mass, m_g gravitational mass.
Abbreviation for local inertial frame; 'local Lorentz frame' when an orthonormal basis is used.

notation_and_conventions.notes: Detailed treatment deferred to Part IV.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Lessons 1-6 are bold bulleted takeaways referenced in later chapters.
e_t denotes the time basis vector of a frame (tangent to the geodesic for a freely falling frame).
g_00 time-time, g_0i time-space, g_ij space-space; Latin indices spatial.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Exercise 6.6 switches to g_tt for the same component.

margin_notes.summary: A freely falling body is defined as one acted on only by gravity.
The weak equivalence principle is called weak because it is restricted to mechanical phenomena; the strong version follows.
Equivalence only holds over a small enough region of space and time; the size is quantified later by tidal effects.
Test particles are assumed light enough that their mutual gravity can be ignored.
Tides come from field differences across a body; oceans respond more than rock, but the Earth tide still stretches the 27 km LEP ring by millimetres and had to be corrected for.
Newton has the Sun pulling the Earth; Einstein has the Earth feeling no force and following a geodesic that orbits the Sun.
A LIF with an orthonormal basis is also called a local Lorentz frame.
The 'sufficiently small' condition of Lesson 3 is the caveat promised in the earlier note.
The rocket bending is not a relativistic effect; the same appears for rain seen from an accelerating car.
Starlight bending was measured early and gave Einstein's ideas their first vindication.
Pointer box: the light-bending calculation is done properly in Section 24.1.
Pointer box: readers eager for the core of GR may skip the Machian interlude to section 6.2.
Centrifugal force is an example of an inertial force; see Chapter 8.
Biographical dates of Ernst Mach (1838-1916).
A quip attributed to Mach by Philipp Frank blames the fixed stars for knocking over subway passengers.
An accelerating charge produces a 1/r force, related to electromagnetic radiation.
Nonlinearity persists even with fields: EM waves pass through each other because they carry no charge, whereas gravitational waves themselves gravitate and interact.
'General relativity' is something of a misnomer, not a more general form of relativity than SR.
F = dp/dt relates vectors without a preferred basis; a law built from one component would be suspicious both dimensionally and in its transformation.
The correct gravity equation will have curvature-related derivatives on the left and the energy-momentum tensor (Section 4.5) on the right.
A tensor equation whose indices match on both sides is called manifestly covariant.
Explains diag(-1,1,1,1) notation for a diagonal 4x4 matrix.
Tensor fields are written T(x) with x a point P or its coordinates.
Because gravity is geometric, speaking of a gravitational force field is unhelpful; the field of the theory is the metric.
The Riemann tensor is defined properly in Chapter 11.
Observers must normalize their local frame to the Lorentz signature.

Frames (basis vectors) differ from coordinates; a general LIF is realized by Riemann normal coordinates (Chapter 35), while the freely falling frame has e_t along a geodesic and stays inertial for long proper times but only over small spatial regions.
Restore c to get the time-dilation factor [1 - 2GM/(c^2 r)]^{1/2}.
The Schwarzschild radius is treated in detail in Part IV.

notable.why_notable: Builds a feel for the enormous range of GM/(Rc^2) across astrophysical objects.

notable.summary: Decide whether a reported frequency gradient across a millimetre-sized cloud of ultracold strontium atoms in an optical lattice clock agrees with the GR prediction.
notable.why_notable: Ties the chapter to a 2022 laboratory measurement of redshift over a millimetre.

notable.summary: Compare a clock on a circular-orbit satellite with one at a planet's pole, including both the gravitational and the orbital-speed effect, find the orbit radius where they agree, and evaluate the difference for a geostationary satellite.
skills: combining SR and GR time dilation
notable.why_notable: The GPS logic in miniature; the neat result r = 3R/2 is a memorable check. The statement calls the planet mass m but uses M in the formula.

notable.summary: Using the Schwarzschild line element, find static-observer proper time and compare wavefront intervals from an atomic transition at one radius as seen at another.
skills: reading g_00 from a line element

difficulty.notes: Main text uses only Newtonian kinematics, a Galilean transformation, index matching, one metric component and a binomial expansion; conceptual load comes from separating local from global statements, frames from coordinates, and from accepting deferred claims (local flatness, Riemann). A few statements are loose or wrong (timelike curves called geodesics, light-bending factor of three) and could mislead careful readers. Exercises 6.5 and 6.6 jump to general stationary metrics and are markedly harder than the chapter.
