teaching_gems.gem: Transform gravity out of an interacting many-particle equation with x' = x - g t^2/2, so the learner sees the g term cancel while pair forces survive.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Turns an abstract principle into a two-line calculation and highlights why universality of free fall (m_i = m_g) is essential.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Equation morph: the Newtonian equation animates term by term under the transformation, with a live particle cloud whose centre-of-mass motion disappears when the frame switch is toggled.

teaching_gems.gem: A uniform field is equivalent to no field, so the only honest evidence for gravity is tidal: release two particles and watch their separation.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Resolves the apparent paradox of the equivalence principle and plants the seed of curvature as relative acceleration.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Unlabeled-cabin challenge where the learner must detect a planet using test particles; the minimum detectable cabin size scales with planet radius.

teaching_gems.gem: Accelerating-rocket crossing shows light must bend, followed by an honest admission that locality fails for the full photon path and spatial curvature supplies more.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Delivers a real prediction from almost no mathematics while modelling scientific candour about the limits of a heuristic.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Two-part demo: rocket frame bending, then a 'full GR' overlay showing the time-part and space-part contributions to solar deflection as equal halves.

teaching_gems.gem: Build a plausible Lorentz-invariant theory of gravity (wave-equation Poisson) and show it fails because density is not a scalar.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learning why a natural guess fails makes the tensor source and curvature feel necessary rather than arbitrary.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Boost slider applied to a dust cloud: rho grows by gamma^2 while a scalar would stay fixed; the learner sees the mismatch between the two sides of the equation.

teaching_gems.gem: Equivalence plus covariance syllogism: a tensor law true without gravity stays true with gravity after eta -> g.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Gives a practical recipe that the learner can immediately apply to Maxwell's equations or conservation laws.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Recipe card interaction: drag an SR equation onto a 'curved spacetime' zone; the app substitutes eta -> g and flags where partial derivatives still need upgrading (bridge to ch7).

teaching_gems.gem: Local flatness as a hierarchy: value and slope of the metric can be matched to Minkowski at a point, curvature (second derivatives) cannot.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Maps onto the familiar Taylor-expansion picture of a tangent plane touching a curved surface.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Sphere with a tangent plane at a draggable point; show the metric error growing quadratically with distance, with coefficient given by curvature.

teaching_gems.gem: Derive gravitational time dilation twice: from g_00 and from a falling clock that uses SR gamma at escape speed.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Two independent routes to the same factor build confidence and link GR clocks to familiar SR dilation and Newtonian energy.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Clock-drop animation with dual readout of (1 - 2GM/rc^2)^{1/2} and 1/gamma(v_fall), including a finite-height release mode revealing the heuristic's assumption.

teaching_gems.gem: Place GR in a square of limits with SR, Newtonian gravity and Newtonian mechanics.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A one-glance map that tells learners what any new theory must reproduce and where each approximation lives.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Interactive regime map (v/c versus GM/rc^2) with real systems plotted and a probe showing the size of neglected terms.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The text states that the full deflection of light by a spherical mass is three times the equivalence-principle estimate and that the argument accounts for one third; the standard result is that the time-part (equivalence) and space-part contributions are equal, so the full value is twice the heuristic (4GM/(bc^2) versus 2GM/(bc^2)).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may memorize the wrong ratio and be confused when ch24 or other sources give a factor of two; it also clashes with the later 'factor of 4' remark relative to the crude estimate.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Teach: equivalence principle (or Newtonian corpuscle) gives 2GM/(bc^2); spatial curvature doubles it to 4GM/(bc^2) = 1.75 arcsec at the solar limb; the crude (6.5) misses a further factor 2 from integrating along the whole path.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 6.3 says timelike curves 'are called geodesics', implying any timelike curve is a geodesic.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Blurs the distinction between accelerated world lines and free fall, which ch8-9 rely on.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say: free-fall world lines are timelike and locally straight (zero 4-acceleration); those special timelike curves are geodesics.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The clock-drop rederivation is heuristic: it assumes the falling clock's rate stays equal to the far clock's, uses reciprocal SR time dilation without specifying which frame measures which clock, and its dt/d tau labelling is inverted relative to (6.11).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Attentive learners notice SR dilation is symmetric and may conclude the argument proves either direction; the exact agreement with Schwarzschild looks deeper than it is.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present it as a plausibility argument; for a rigorous route use g_00 or photon energy conservation (Pound-Rebka style climb) and later the Killing-energy argument in Schwarzschild.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise 6.5 eqn (6.16) is labelled the proper time at A but equals the coordinate-time round trip; without a factor (-g_00)^{1/2} it does not lead to (6.17).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Students attempting part (d) cannot reproduce the stated spatial metric and may doubt their algebra.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use d tau = 2[(g_0i g_0j - g_ij g_00)dx^i dx^j]^{1/2}/(-g_00)^{1/2} and dl = d tau/2 (c = 1).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Minor printed slips in exercises: Exercise 6.3 names the planet mass m but the result uses M; eqn (6.19) omits d phi inside the integral; (6.20) is in c = 1 units.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Small but can stall a novice checking dimensions.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Tutor should silently correct: mass M, integrand with d phi, and Delta N = 4 pi Omega r^2/(lambda c) in SI.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The local flatness theorem's first condition is justified only by 'a symmetric matrix can be diagonalized', and the vanishing of first derivatives is asserted without the counting argument.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers may think diagonalizing at a point is trivially the whole story and not see why second derivatives cannot vanish (20 leftover degrees of freedom = Riemann components).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add the Taylor-expansion counting: 10 metric values vs 16 Jacobian entries, 40 first derivatives vs 40 second-order coefficients, 100 second derivatives vs 80 third-order coefficients; defer proof to ch35.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Fig. 6.4 labels the GR-to-Newtonian-gravity limit only as v -> 0, but the Newtonian limit also requires weak fields (GM/rc^2 << 1) and stresses small compared with energy density; G -> 0 for SR is also more naturally 'curvature negligible'.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think slow motion near a black hole is Newtonian.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Relabel axes as v/c and GM/(rc^2) (or c -> infinity) and emphasize both conditions for the Newtonian limit.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: General covariance is presented as having strong physical content and as a restatement of the equivalence principle; the Kretschmann objection (any theory can be written covariantly) is not mentioned.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Advanced learners may later find the principle's status contested and feel misled.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Frame covariance as a powerful guiding heuristic that, combined with 'no prior geometry' and minimal coupling, constrains theories; mention the debate briefly for advanced learners.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The eta -> g rule (Lesson 4) omits that derivatives must also become covariant derivatives, and that curvature-coupling ambiguities can arise for second-derivative laws.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A learner applying the rule literally to partial_mu T^{mu nu} = 0 gets a non-tensorial equation.

tutor_notes: Open with a question: 'If you were in a windowless box, could you tell whether you are resting on Earth or accelerating at 9.8 m/s^2 in deep space?' Then: 'What if the box were very large?' The second question leads directly to tides.

Order of explanation that works: m_i = m_g and universality of free fall -> transforming away uniform g (Example 6.1) -> accelerometer in free fall reads zero -> strong principle and LIFs -> tides as the invariant remnant -> light bending as a payoff -> covariance and eta -> g -> metric as field and local flatness -> clock rates.
Check for understanding: ask the learner why an orbiting astronaut is weightless even though gravity at ISS altitude is about 90 percent of surface gravity.
Check: ask which of two initially side-by-side particles above a planet move together or apart, then repeat for a vertically stacked pair; expect converge and diverge respectively.
When covering light bending, correct the text's factor: the equivalence-principle argument yields half the GR deflection (not one third); the full solar-limb value is 1.75 arcsec.

For Example 6.7 have the learner boost a cloud of dust: number density gains a gamma and each particle's energy gains a gamma, so energy density scales as gamma^2, making it clear rho is not a scalar.
Distinguish 'local inertial frame at an event' (g = eta, dg = 0 there) from 'freely falling frame along a world line'; learners often conflate them.

For time dilation, emphasize comparison by signals: each clock ticks normally for its owner; the redshift is a relation between separated observers. Use GPS numbers (+45, -7, net +38 microseconds per day) as a memorable anchor.

Common learner question: 'If gravity is not a force, why do I feel it standing on the ground?' Answer: the ground's normal force pushes you off your geodesic; what you feel is that non-gravitational force.
Common learner question: 'Why can't we transform away curvature too?' Use the tangent-plane picture: you can match height and slope of a surface at a point but not its bending.

Common learner question: 'Is general relativity just about accelerated frames?' No: SR already handles accelerated observers; GR is about gravity as curvature, and the name comes from general covariance.

Adapt by level: for novices stay with elevators, rockets, tides and clock comparisons with numbers; for advanced learners add the derivative-counting argument for local flatness, the EEP/SEP distinction, and the exact Schwarzschild status of (6.11).
